name: Adam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a package holiday company, on the team that handles changes, so name changes, date changes, people who missed a flight. It's phones in the morning and chat in the afternoon, from a contact centre on the top floor of an old department store in town. In summer it's chaos, everyone's flight is delayed at once. I like the fixing, finding a hotel at midnight for a family stuck at the airport.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how do you work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About eight months, so I'm still learning the booking system, which is ancient. I use AI for basically everything, I've got my own prompts saved for refund emails and I paste the airline rules in to get a quick summary. My team leader says my scores are below average because I take too long on chats, but I'm getting there. I live with two flatmates in a terraced house near the station, and I've got about two weeks of money saved, if that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. That would surprise me, I use it every day and it's getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I still think it's handy, even if it's not the revolution. At work I'd keep showing people my prompts. Online I'd probably say the hype people got it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Job-wise I'm probably fine, holidays still go wrong and people still ring us. The issue is my pay, which is barely more than the supermarket, and there's not much else in town for someone like me. If I'm honest, I'm here because nothing better came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get my chat times down using the AI more cleverly. I'd ask if I could help train new starters on the system, because that's a route up. And I'd set up a little side thing helping guesthouses near the coast with their booking replies, for a few hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit bored, if anything. Fine but flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A side thing with guesthouses. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are loads of small places that take bookings by email and never reply on time. I could set them up with AI replies and a simple calendar for, say, a hundred and fifty each. My aunt runs one, so I'd start with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing better came up. What would better look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where I'm building stuff, not just answering. Maybe a job setting up systems for the company. I'm not picky about the title, I just want to stop being on a queue.

say: I'd say AI is **still handy**, even if it's not a revolution.
At work I'd keep sharing my **prompts** with colleagues.
think: His job is **probably fine** because holidays keep going wrong.
His pay is **barely above supermarket** level, with few better local jobs.
do: Use AI more cleverly to bring his **chat times** down.
Ask to help **train new starters** on the booking system.
Help **guesthouses** set up AI booking replies for a few hundred a month.
S0.quote: I just want to stop being on a queue.
fieldNote: He is already an **everyday AI user** and sees it as his way up.
His worry is **low pay** and few options, not job loss.
The guesthouse idea starts with his **aunt**, keeping risk small.

steps.text: Keep working the holiday changes team
Build saved prompts to cut his chat handling time
Set up AI booking replies for his aunt's guesthouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking and answering customers. So my job, twice over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and the people who learn it will be fine. I'd be the one at work showing people how to use the tools. I'd also say the company needs to be fair about who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, half my team goes, maybe more, because a bot can rebook a flight faster than us. I think I'd be in a better spot than most, because I'm the one who actually knows the tools. But I'm also new and below average on scores, so it could go either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager to put me on whatever team sets up the new booking bot, even as a tester. I'd do a free online course on automation tools in the evenings. And I'd grow the guesthouse thing to five or six clients, so I've got something if the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Nervous but kind of buzzing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company doesn't want you on that team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go freelance faster, setting up booking systems for small places. It's risky with two weeks of savings, I know. I'd probably keep a part-time job at the supermarket to cover rent while I build it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a guy called Phil who's been there nine years and hates new screens. He's brilliant with angry customers, but he'd be one of the first out. I'd try to show him the tools, but he'd tell me to get lost.

say: I'd say people who **learn the tools** will be fine.
I'd ask the company to be **fair** about who goes.
think: **Half his team** goes because a bot rebooks flights faster.
He's the **tools person** but also new and low-scoring, so it could go either way.

fieldNote: He sees the change as a **chance** but admits his scores make him vulnerable.

He worries for an older colleague who **won't adapt**.

steps.text: Volunteer as a tester for the company's new booking bot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's different. That's not a wave, that's a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and we need sensible rules fast, things like support for people who lose jobs. I'd be posting guides on how to use the new tools, because that's what I do. But I wouldn't pretend I had it all worked out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and my side thing both die. If AI can do any thinking work, guesthouses don't need me to set it up, they just ask it. The only work left for a few years would be hands-on, until the robots in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the guesthouse work hard for the first year while people still feel they need help. Then I'd look at hands-on jobs where I'm useful, like installing solar panels or doing removals. I'd ask my flatmates about cheaper rent, or move to a smaller room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Everything I thought was my edge is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've used AI more than most. Does that help at all in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a year. I'd understand what's happening faster than most people, which is something. But understanding AI doesn't pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine and I've got a plan, even if I don't. She worries enough. I'd tell her I was going into solar panels and make it sound exciting.

say: I'd call for **sensible rules** and support for people who lose jobs.
I'd post **guides** on using the new tools.
think: His job and **side business** both die when AI does any thinking work.
Only **hands-on work** lasts a few years, until robots around 2031.
do: Push the **guesthouse work** hard for the first year.
Look at hands-on jobs like **solar panel** installing or removals.
Ask his flatmates about **cheaper rent** or a smaller room.
fieldNote: He recognises that **fast AGI** removes the advantage he built.
He'd hide the worry from his **mum** and make it sound exciting.
He switches quickly to **hands-on** options, true to his adaptive style.

steps.text: Sell AI booking set-ups to guesthouses for one year
Apply for solar panel installer or removals jobs
Swap to the smallest room in the shared house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to actually ride it for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a window, so use it. I'd tell everyone at work to get good with the tools now. I'd also say the government should make it easy to retrain, because not everyone's like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three good years out of being the AI person, on the company's automation team or freelancing. After 2031 the thinking work is gone, so I'd want a hands-on trade by then. Robots come around 2034, which gives me a few years in that trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the bot project at work in the first year and push the guesthouse work to ten clients. I'd save the extra money, aiming for three months of rent. Then around year two, I'd start a solar installer course, so I'm ready to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but focused. Like the night before a big exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten clients and a full-time job. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not ten, but six or seven. I work fast once something's set up. I'd lose my weekends for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why solar specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every roof in town will want panels, and solar is not something a chatbot does. It's outdoors and physical. My cousin did it and earns more than I do.

say: I'd say there's **a window**, so use it.
I'd call for **easy retraining**, because not everyone adapts like him.
think: He expects **three good years** as the AI person at work or freelancing.
He needs a **hands-on trade** before 2031, with robots around 2034.
do: Join the **bot project** at work and grow guesthouse clients.
Start a **solar installer** course around year two.
feel: **Nervous but focused**, like the night before a big exam.
S3.quote: Every roof in town will want panels, and solar is not something a chatbot does.
fieldNote: He plans a **two-step move**: AI work first, then a trade.

He'd sacrifice **weekends** for a while to build the side business.

steps.text: Join the company's booking bot project in year one
Grow guesthouse AI set-ups to six or seven clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career and a half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and people should take it seriously, not panic. I'd be talking about it at work all the time, probably annoying people. I'd say learn the tools now and pick a trade for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine for most of that decade. The call centre job probably goes by 2030 anyway, but by then I'd be on the automation side or running my own little business. The end point bugs me, though, because the robots come in 2039 and I'd be thirty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move onto the automation team at work in the first year and keep growing the guesthouse business. I'd start saving properly, maybe putting a small amount into an index fund. And I'd keep an eye on trades, so I can switch when the time's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, a bit restless. The end of the story is the bit I can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An index fund on two weeks of savings. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. First I'd get three months of rent saved. Then twenty a month into a fund, just to start the habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock this plan off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company shuts the centre and moves everything abroad or to an AI firm overnight. Then I'm out with no notice. That's the one thing ten years doesn't protect you from.

I'd tell people to **learn the tools** now and pick a trade for later.

The **2039** robot end point still bothers him.

Save **three months** of rent, then put twenty a month into an **index fund**.
Keep watching **trades** to switch at the right time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because everything I'm good at stops mattering overnight. What would help is fast, free training in trades for people my age, and some kind of payment while you train, because I can't live on nothing for a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what happens to the people who aren't into tech. I'll probably find a way, but my colleague who's been there nine years won't. Someone needs a plan for people like him.

headlineQuote: Everything I'm good at stops mattering overnight.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** agent on a holiday company's **changes team**, eight months in and still learning the booking system.
He uses **AI daily**, with saved prompts, and wants to stop being on a queue.
He rents a room in a **shared house** and has about two weeks of savings.
He is **pragmatic** and adaptive, building a side business setting up AI booking replies for guesthouses.
He rides AI in the slower pictures but plans to switch to **solar installing** before robots arrive.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because everything he's good at **stops mattering**.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, free **trade training** for people his age.
A **payment** while training, since he can't go a year without income.
